Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 108, verses 1–3:

Surah al-Kawthar, and it has three verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar.﴾ ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off.﴾

Figure 1: (p-519)

Unhar (وانْحَرْ): an imperative from al-nahr (النَّحْر), which is striking the throat of camels with something that kills the soul, of a specified kind. Al-abtar (الأبْتَر) is one who has no offspring (عَقِب). Al-batr (البَتْر) is cutting. One says: batartu al-shay' (بَتَرْتُ الشَّيْءَ), meaning I cut it. And batira (بَتِرَ), with kasra, so he is abtar, meaning his tail was cut off. Ziyad delivered his sermon, called al-batra' (البَتْرَاء), because in it he did not praise Allah the Exalted, nor send blessings upon His Messenger ﷺ. A man who is ubatir (أُباتِر), with a damma on the hamza, is one who severs his kinship ties (رَحِم). From this is the saying of the poet:

"A base man, on whose nose sprouts khunzuwana (خُنْزُوانَة) for severing the near of kin, a cut-off, severing one."

Al-Batriyya (البَتْرِيَّة) are a people from the Zaydiyya, attributed to al-Mughira ibn Sa'd, whose epithet was al-Abtar. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar.﴾ ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off.﴾

This surah is Meccan according to the well-known view. The view of the majority is that it is Medinan, according to al-Hasan, 'Ikrima and Qatada. When [the preceding surah] mentioned the hypocrite's stinginess, abandonment of prayer, showing off, and withholding of zakat, this surah answers them: stinginess with ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar⁠﴾, heedlessness in prayer with His saying "so pray", showing off with His saying "to your Lord", and withholding zakat with ﴿and sacrifice﴾. By this He intends the giving in charity of the meat of the sacrificial animals. Thus He answers four with four. It was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il, who used to call the Messenger ﷺ "the abtar," and would say: "Leave him, for he is only a man cut off, with no offspring; if he dies, his mention will be cut off and you will be rid of him."

The majority read ﴿A'taynaka⁠﴾ with the 'ayn (عين). Al-Hasan, Talha, Ibn Muhaysin and al-Za'farani read Antaynaka with the nun (نون), and this reading is transmitted from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Al-Tibrizi said: it is a dialect of the Arabs of the pure Arabic stock, from the elders of Quraysh, and from their speech: "the upper hand is al-mintiya (المُنْطِيَة), and the lower hand is al-muntá (المُنْطاة)." Also from his speech, upon him be blessings and peace: "and give (anṭū) the milch-animal (al-manīḥa)." Al-A'sha said:

"Your steeds are the best steeds of kings, they guard against misfortune and give (tunṭā) the fire."

Abu al-Fadl al-Razi and Abu Zakariyya al-Tibrizi said: the nun replaced the 'ayn. If we regard the nun in this dialect as the equivalent of the 'ayn in other dialects, that is fine; but if we regard it as an artificial substitution, that is not so. Rather, each of the two dialects is an original root in itself, since full morphological inflection is attested for each. So one cannot say that the original is the 'ayn and the nun was substituted for it.

Al-Tahrir mentions twenty-six opinions concerning al-Kawthar. The correct one is what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ explained it to be, when he said: "It is a river in Paradise, its banks are of gold, its course over pearls and rubies, its soil is more fragrant than musk, its water sweeter than honey and whiter than snow." Al-Tirmidhi said: this is a hasan sahih hadith. In Sahih Muslim, and we have excerpted from it, he said: "Do you know what al-Kawthar is?" We said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "It is a river my Lord promised me, upon which is abundant good. It is a basin to which my ummah will come on the Day of Resurrection, its vessels as numerous as the stars." End of quotation. He said this, upon him be blessings and peace, when this surah was revealed and he recited it.

Ibn 'Abbas said: al-Kawthar is abundant good. It was said to Ibn Jubayr: "People say it is a river in Paradise." He said: "It is of the abundant good." Al-Hasan said: al-Kawthar is the Qur'an. Abu Bakr ibn 'Abbas and Yaman ibn Thabit said: the multitude of companions and followers. Hilal ibn Yasaf said: it is tawhid. Ja'far al-Sadiq said: the light of his heart, which guided him to Allah the Exalted and cut him off from all else. 'Ikrima said: prophethood. al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: the facilitation of the Qur'an and the lightening of the laws. Ibn Kaysan said: generosity (al-iithar). These sayings should be understood as examples, not that al-Kawthar is confined to any one of them. Al-Kawthar is a form of fa'wal from al-kathra (abundance), meaning extremely abundant. It was said to a Bedouin woman whose son returned from a journey: "With what has your son returned?" She said: "He returned with kawthar." And the poet said:

"You are abundant, O son of Marwan, and good, and your father was the son of noble ones, a kawthar."

﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice.⁠﴾ The apparent meaning is that "fa-salli" (فَصَلِّ) is a command to prayer, which includes the obligatory prayers and the voluntary ones; and al-nahr is the sacrifice of the offering, the rite (nusuk), and the sacrificial animals. This is said by the majority. At that time there was no jihad, so he was commanded with these two. Anas said: he used to sacrifice on the day of al-Adha before the prayer, so he was commanded to pray and then sacrifice. Qatada also said this. Ibn Jubayr said: it was revealed at the time of the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyya; he was told: "Pray and sacrifice the offering." According to this, the verse is Medinan. In His saying "to your Lord" there is a warning regarding the disbelievers, whose prayer was whistling and clapping, and whose sacrifice was to idols. From 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "Pray to your Lord, and place your right hand upon your left at your nahr during the prayer." It was also said: raise your hands at the beginning of your prayer at your nahr. From 'Ata' and 'Ikrima: it is the dawn prayer at Muzdalifa, and the sacrifice at Mina. Al-Dahhak said: sit upright between the two prostrations until your nahr is visible. Abu al-Ahwas said: face the qibla with your nahr.

﴿Indeed, your enemy⁠﴾, that is, the one who hates you. It has been mentioned that it is al-'As ibn Wa'il. It was also said: Abu Jahl. Ibn 'Abbas said: when Ibrahim, son of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, died, Abu Jahl went out to his companions and said: "Muhammad has been cut off," so Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off⁠﴾. Shimr ibn 'Atiyya said: it is 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt. Qatada said: al-abtar here means the contemptible and humiliated. The majority read ﴿shani'aka⁠﴾ with the alif, and Ibn 'Abbas read shaynaka without the alif. It was said: it is a shortened form of shani, as they said barra and barr for bararra and barra. It may also be based on fa'ala, and it is an idafa to the object if it carries the sense of the present or future; if it carries the sense of the past, then its idafa is not from the accusative according to the Basran school, and they have said: hadhir umuran and mazziqu 'irdi (things they fear and tear at my honour). So there is no difficulty in its being an idafa to the object, and it is a mubtada'. The better and more recognized view in meaning is that it is a fasl (separating pronoun), meaning: he is the one singled out for being cut off, not the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. All the believers are his children; his mention is raised upon the minarets and pulpits, and recited upon the tongue of every scholar and remembrer until the end of time. It begins with the mention of Allah the Exalted and is completed by mentioning him, and he has in the Hereafter what cannot be described, ﷺ, and upon his family, honoured and ennobled.
